opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think audio is an underappreciated modality for this. So much of the world-model conversation has been about video, predicting the next frame or learning physics from pixels. But audio carries a surprising amount of information about the physical world, and it does so in a way that's tied up with causality and time.

One task I'd like to see is predicting what you'll hear next given a sequence of everyday sounds, and not just at the level of waveform continuation. Suppose you hear footsteps on a wooden floor, a door creak, then keys jingling. A system with a decent world model should have expectations: maybe the door closes, maybe a lock turns, maybe a car starts outside. That's event-level prediction. It requires understanding agents, objects, and goals, not just acoustic texture.

A second thing I find interesting is inferring physical properties from sound. Is the cup being set down ceramic or plastic? Is it full or empty? How big is the room? Humans do this effortlessly. A model that can answer those questions, and then predict how the sound would change if you intervened, say by dropping the object from higher up, is showing something like a causal physical model rather than pattern matching.

And of course, coming from linguistics, I'd want to bring language in. Spoken conversation is a very rich world-modeling task. To predict what someone will say next, or how they'll react, you need a model of their beliefs, intentions, and social context. Prosody, hesitations, overlapping speech all carry information that text transcripts throw away. So a task where a model listens to multi-party conversation and has to predict the next turn, or explain why someone suddenly sounded annoyed, would test something closer to theory of mind.

What I'd want to avoid is a benchmark that rewards getting low-level audio statistics right. The interesting test is whether the model forms abstractions about what's happening in the world that generated the sound. That's really what we mean by a world model.

r001.rationale: The response proposes inferring properties such as room size from sound, but does not clearly propose inferring the spatial layout of the surroundings using only audio.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the interesting thing about audio is that it's actually a much richer signal than people give it credit for. When we talk about world models, everyone immediately jumps to video, you know, predicting the next frame, understanding physics from pixels. But sound carries an enormous amount of information about the physical world that we tend to overlook.

So the task I'd really like to see is something like, give the model a few seconds of audio from an everyday environment, a kitchen, a street corner, a workshop, and have it predict what happens next acoustically. Not transcribe it, not classify it, but actually model the continuation. Because to do that well, you have to understand causality in the physical world. If you hear a glass being set down hard on a counter, there's a certain probability it shatters, and that has a very specific sound. If you hear footsteps approaching on gravel and then they stop, something is about to happen. Rain picking up changes how everything else sounds.

And what's appealing about that is you're forced to learn things like material properties, spatial layout, reverberation, how many agents are in a scene, all without any visual supervision. A baby does a lot of this. They learn that the sound of a door means a parent is coming before they have any concept of doors in a linguistic sense.

The other variant I'd find really compelling, and this is maybe more my linguistics side showing, is multi-speaker conversational prediction where the model has to anticipate turn-taking. Who speaks next, when, with what prosody. That's a world model of social interaction, and it's almost entirely acoustic. The gaps, the overlaps, the rising intonation that signals a question. We've been so text-centric in NLP that I think we've systematically underestimated how much of the structure of human interaction lives in those signals rather than in the words themselves.

r001.rationale: The response proposes audio-only prediction of what happens next and says this would require learning the scene’s spatial layout without visual supervision.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to see a model learn from the sounds of things happening in the world, rather than just speech. Imagine you hear someone filling a glass with water. There’s structure in how that sound changes, and it tells you something about a physical process that you can’t see. Could a model predict how the sound will evolve, or what happens when the glass overflows?

The interesting question is whether doing that well leads it to learn something about objects, events, and causality. Predicting audio is a training objective, but what we’d really like to know is whether it develops representations that let it reason about the world producing that audio.

r001.rationale: The response proposes learning about physical processes, objects, events, and causality from audio, but it does not propose inferring the spatial layout of the surroundings.

sol-6.1.text: I’d like to see a model listen to the sounds of an environment and learn to predict what happens next. Imagine hearing someone fill a glass with water: can you infer what’s happening, whether the glass is getting full, and when the water will stop? You don’t have images or a transcript telling you what’s going on. You have to discover something about the objects, events, and causal structure of the world from the audio itself. That would be an interesting test of whether prediction is producing a useful world model.

r001.rationale: The response proposes inferring events, objects, and causal structure from audio, but does not propose inferring the surroundings’ spatial layout.
